deep.reconstruction:
This is the closing paragraph (§120) of E260, where Euler applies his pipe-friction theory to fountains fed by long conduits. In his model the resisting force on the water is proportional to the pressure the water exerts on the pipe wall. That makes it a Coulomb- or Amontons-type friction law carried over to fluids. Integrating along a pipe of length b and diameter a, with n = b/a, the jet height that would be q without friction becomes Nq, with N<1 decreasing in n. From the table in §119, N ≈ 4000/n for large n.

Because the wall pressure is the absolute pressure, atmospheric pressure also generates friction. Its effect is an extra subtractive height M, the water-column equivalent of the atmosphere, which Euler takes as 30 ft. Hence v = Nq − M. For n > 50000 this becomes v ≈ (4000 a/b) q − 30 ft.

The numbers check against §118. With b = 25000 ft and a = 1/4 ft, n = 100000 and N = 1/25. Then q must exceed 25·30 = 750 ft for any jet at all. q = 1000 gives v = 10 ft, q = 2000 gives v = 50 ft, and each extra 1000 ft of head adds 40 ft.

Euler then draws a testable conclusion. Since M is proportional to barometric height, a fountain should rise higher when the barometer is low.
errors: The physical conclusion is false. Under the real (viscous/turbulent) pipe-friction law, losses depend on velocity, not on absolute pressure. Atmospheric pressure acts equally on the reservoir surface and on the jet exit, so it cancels from incompressible flow. Fountain height does not grow as the barometer falls. The error comes straight from Euler's hypothesis that fluid friction is proportional to wall pressure.
Notation slip: the formula is printed as 4000 d/b, but the quotient was defined as n = b/a. The symbol should be a (the pipe diameter), so N ≈ 4000/n = 4000a/b.

The threshold here (n > 50000) does not match §119, where the approximation N = 1/ν with n = 4000ν is stated for ν > 5, i.e. n > 20000. The two statements are only loosely consistent (this one is a stricter condition), not a contradiction.
M = 30 ft is a rounded water-barometer height; the actual value is about 32–34 ft depending on units. This is harmless.

ideas.what: Fluid friction in pipes taken as proportional to wall pressure, including atmospheric pressure, giving jet height v = Nq − M
ideas.modern_name: Coulomb/Amontons-type friction hypothesis applied to pipe flow (since superseded by Darcy–Weisbach velocity-dependent losses)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (E260), discussed as an unsuccessful early attempt in histories of hydraulics
ideas.where_published: E260, Novi Commentarii Petrop. 6 (1761); Opera omnia II.12/13 and editors' introductions (Truesdell)

ideas.what: Asymptotic law N ≈ 4000 a/b for long pipes: delivered head inversely proportional to the length-to-diameter ratio
ideas.modern_name: Head loss scaling with L/D (qualitatively like Darcy–Weisbach)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Prony, Darcy, Weisbach for the modern form

ideas.what: Prediction that fountains rise higher at low barometric pressure
ideas.modern_name: Falsifiable consequence of a pressure-proportional friction law

missed.claim: Euler's own friction model yields an explicit, experimentally testable (and false) prediction: jet height should rise as barometric pressure falls. Such a test could have refuted the pressure-proportional friction hypothesis. It is rarely highlighted as a falsifiable prediction in accounts of the prehistory of pipe-friction laws.
missed.quote: sequitur fontes salientes ad eo maiorem altitudinem ascendere debere, quo minus mercurius in Barometro fuerit eleuatus
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is of historical interest only, as an illustration of how a wrong constitutive law produced a checkable prediction. It has no mathematical novelty.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a routine application of the paper's (physically mistaken) friction law, ending with a barometric corollary. E260's friction hypothesis is known and discussed in the Opera omnia commentary, and nothing mathematically new appears here.
transcription_corrections: 'ad eo' in the scan is the old spelling of 'adeo'.
In the formula the image shows '4000 d / b · q − 30'. It is transcribed correctly, but the 'd' (possibly a misprint for 'a') should be read as the pipe diameter a, consistent with n = b/a.
